svg.aria-label: Diagram: what the SAML single sign-on exchange actually verifies, why super admins are exempt from single sign-on and therefore outside any multi-factor policy the external identity provider enforces, a discrepancy between two Google documentation pages about identity-provider-initiated sign-on, and what carries over from the previous two posts about reused email addresses
svg.title: Single sign-on: what the assertion proves, and which accounts it does not cover
svg.text: Federation moves authentication out. It does not move it for everyone.
The accounts exempt from single sign-on are the ones that can change the whole organization.
What the exchange actually verifies
1. The signature on the assertion, against the public key in your SSO configuration.
2. The audience, so the assertion was issued for Google and not somewhere else.
3. The NameID, matched to the PRIMARY EMAIL ADDRESS of a user account.
That is the whole check. The IdP is free to use whatever logic it likes to derive the NameID.
The accounts with the most power are the ones SSO does not cover
All users EXCEPT super admins are forced to use single sign-on.
Super admins are not redirected to your IdP; they are prompted for username and password.
So any MFA your external IdP enforces does not apply to them. Enforce Google 2-step instead.
Deliberate, and defensible: it is how you get back in when the IdP is down or the config is wrong.
Two Google pages disagree about IdP-initiated sign-on. Read both.
Single sign-on (reviewed 2025-07-30): Google does not support this flow.
Best practices (reviewed 2024-07-11): super admins are still allowed to use SSO when the IdP
initiates it, and are therefore sensitive to name squatting with no IdP counterpart.
Both cannot be current. The mitigation is cheap either way, so apply it regardless.
What carries over from #49 and #50
A reused address is the same identity to federation: a joiner can inherit the data, settings and
permissions of the leaver. And if SSO is ever disabled, defunct accounts can be used again.
Also: the sync tool from #50 runs as a machine super-admin, an account SSO does not protect.
SSO moves authentication to your IdP. It does not move authorization, and it does not cover
super admins. The allow policy still decides what the resulting session is allowed to do.
#50 gave the referent a delete button. #51 shows the front door has a documented side entrance,
held open on purpose, for exactly the accounts that can change everything.
